items.title: Italy's former police chief rejected mafia inquiry allegations before death
items.summary: The contents of an eight-page letter by Gianni De Gennaro have been revealed days after his body was found at his Tuscany home.
items.body:
Image source, Reuters

Image caption,

Gianni De Gennaro worked in the anti-mafia directorate and became police chief before he headed Italian defence company Finmeccanica, later renamed Leonardo

ByDavide Ghiglione, in Rome and Laura Gozzi

Italian ex-police chief Gianni De Gennaro has denied misleading investigations into high-profile Mafia killings, in a letter written shortly before his death.

His body was found at his Tuscan country home on Saturday and Italian authorities believe he took his own life. A post mortem examination was due to take place on Friday.

In his eight-page note, De Gennaro, 78, vehemently denied obstructing the inquiry into the murder of anti-mafia judge Paolo Borsellino in Sicily in July 1992.

The Cosa Nostra Mafia was found to have ordered Borsellino's killing and that of fellow judge Giovanni Falcone two months earlier.

But several fruitless investigations were later launched into potential cover-ups by high-ranking officials.

In a recent inquiry De Gennaro, who in the 1990s worked in the anti-mafia directorate and later became Italy's police chief, was accused of misdirecting the initial investigation.

The allegations shocked many Italians, as De Gennaro had worked closely with Falcone and was seen as being on the front line of the fight against organised crime.

"In a few minutes I will be gone, so you understand well that a 'man condemned to death' cannot lie," he wrote in the letter, published by Italian daily Corriere della Sera. "I have never betrayed my oath of loyalty to the Fatherland."

Image source, Getty Images

Image caption,

Gianni De Gennaro (L) and anti-mafia judge Giovanni Falcone in 1992

"I hope that, amid the avalanche of falsehoods now overwhelming me, the truth will ultimately prevail," he added.

The case, and the media furore that has surrounded it, have re-opened the wound of the Mafia killings of the early 1990s, which remain an emotionally charged issue in Italy.

The story has dominated Italian headlines since De Gennaro's death, with several of the country's most senior political figures publicly commenting on the case.

On Thursday Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni said she had been "deeply shocked" by the case.

"His words struck us deeply, and I think the most important think we can do now is to help prosecutors who are working to clear things up," she added.

The letter was found next to a hard drive which he said contained notes from his 40-year career.

According to Italian media, investigators seized two hard drives, one from the home of De Gennaro's son and one from a former member of his security detail, and two USB sticks held by a close collaborator, who is also under investigation.

The sticks are reportedly labelled "Stato-Mafia", a likely reference to the alleged relationship between the Italian state and the Mafia, and "Massacres".

Forensic specialists are now expected to examine whether any files on the hard drives or USB sticks were altered or deleted, reports say.

items.summary: Iran warned South Korea that an expanded foreign military presence in the Gulf could heighten tensions and widen the conflict.

Iran warns on Gulf military presence as South Korea readies expanded naval role

Iran warned South Korea that an expanded foreign military presence in the Gulf could heighten tensions and widen the conflict.

File photo. Iran’s Foreign Minister, Abbas Araqchi, attends a press conference during the 81st United Nations General Assembly (UNGA), at UN headquarters in New York City, US, Sep 25, 2026. (Photo: Reuters/Bing Guan)

SEOUL: Iran's foreign minister has told his South Korean counterpart that a foreign military presence in the Gulf region would heighten tensions rather than contribute to peace, as Seoul prepares to expand the operational area of a navy unit to waters south of the Gulf of Oman.

Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi spoke by telephone on Thursday (Nov 26) with South Korea's Cho Hyun, who reaffirmed Seoul did not intend to join any war or deploy troops to the Gulf, the Iranian embassy in Seoul said in an X post on Friday.

South Korea's parliament is reviewing a government motion to broaden the operating area of its Cheonghae naval unit to include the outer waters of the Gulf of Oman to help ensure safe navigation of its commercial vessels.

The anti-piracy Cheonghae unit has been stationed in the Gulf of Aden since 2009.

Araqchi said the presence of foreign militaries "would instead heighten tensions and expand the scope of conflict", the Iranian embassy said.

South Korea's Foreign Ministry said Cho explained that the mission of the navy unit was to ensure the safety of South Koreans and protect the country's economic interests.

South Korea, which is one of the world's largest oil and gas importers, sourced 70 per cent of its oil from the Middle East in 2025, with most shipments delivered through the Strait of Hormuz, according to government data.

South Korea's Lee rules out military involvement in Middle East conflict

items.title: Strobe Talbott, former Time magazine reporter and deputy secretary of state, has died
items.summary: Strobe Talbott, a former Time magazine reporter who later served as deputy secretary of state under President Bill Clinton and then headed the Brookings Institution, died Thursday. He was 80.
items.body:
Obituaries

Strobe Talbott, former Time magazine reporter and deputy secretary of state, has died

November 27, 20261:12 AM ET

By

The Associated Press

FILE - Strobe Talbott, President Brookings Institution, speaks during a news conference in Berlin, July 16, 2008.

Franka Bruns/AP

hide caption

Franka Bruns/AP

Strobe Talbott, a former Time magazine reporter who later served as deputy secretary of state under President Bill Clinton and then headed the Brookings Institution, died Thursday. He was 80.

His son, Devin Talbott, confirmed he passed away peacefully after a long illness in his East Hampton, New York, home.

The elder Talbott was educated at Yale and Oxford, where he bunked with Clinton. While at the British university, after interning for Time in Moscow, the magazine asked Talbott to help translate the leaked memoirs of Nikita Khrushchev, the former first secretary of the Communist Party of the Soviet Union who was ousted in 1964.

FILE - President-elect Bill Clinton and Strobe Talbott of Time magazine talk privately as they walk along the beach on Hilton Head Island, S.C., Jan. 2, 1993.

James Finley/AP

hide caption

James Finley/AP

Talbott did, and it gave him some notoriety as a young man and a job at the magazine.

After 21 years at Time, where he focused on Soviet-American relations and held positions including Washington bureau chief and a foreign-affairs columnist, according to his U.S. State Department biography, he received a call from the newly elected Clinton.

Talbott joined the U.S. State Department in 1994, swiftly becoming deputy secretary of state. In that role, he was the architect of the Clinton administration's approach to Russia and other formerly Soviet countries and conducted negotiations between the U.S. and India after the latter's nuclear tests in 1998.

"Strobe was a good and brilliant man who made our world more peaceful and secure," said Clinton in a statement after Talbott's death. When Talbott was translating Khrushchev's memoirs while at Oxford, it was Clinton's job to make him breakfast every day, he said, adding, "somehow, I got the better end of the deal."

Both he and Hillary were "deeply saddened" by the passing of "a wonderful friend, and a world-class human being," he said.

Afterward, he served as the president of Brookings from 2002 to 2017. In that time, he also chaired the U.S. State Department's Foreign Affairs Policy Board.

Talbott also authored over a dozen books. His last book was titled "Our Founders' Warning: The Age of Reason Meets the Age of Trump," which was published in 2020.

He was born in Dayton, Ohio, in 1946, and is survived by two sons, Devin and Adrian, and six grandchildren.

His first wife, Brook Shearer, died in 2009, and he later married author Barbara Lazear Ascher.

translation.body:
讣告

前《时代》杂志记者、副国务卿斯特罗布·塔尔博特去世

2026年11月27日 凌晨1:12（美国东部时间）

作者

美联社

资料图——2008年7月16日，布鲁金斯学会主席斯特罗布·塔尔博特在柏林出席一场新闻发布会时发言。

Franka Bruns/美联社

隐藏图注

Franka Bruns/美联社

斯特罗布·塔尔博特，曾任《时代》杂志记者，后于比尔·克林顿总统任内担任副国务卿，之后又执掌布鲁金斯学会，于周四去世，享年80岁。

其子德文·塔尔博特证实，他在纽约州东汉普顿的家中久病之后安详离世。

老塔尔博特曾就读于耶鲁大学和牛津大学，在牛津期间与克林顿同住。在英国求学时，他曾在《时代》杂志莫斯科分社实习，随后该杂志请她协助翻译尼基塔·赫鲁晓夫泄露的回忆录。赫鲁晓夫是苏联共产党前第一书记，于1964年被赶下台。

资料图——1993年1月2日，当选总统比尔·克林顿与《时代》杂志的斯特罗布·塔尔博特在南卡罗来纳州希尔顿黑德岛的海滩上散步时私下交谈。

James Finley/美联社

隐藏图注

James Finley/美联社

塔尔博特完成了这项工作，这让他年纪轻轻便小有名气，并因此获得了该杂志的一份工作。

据美国国务院为其撰写的传记，他在《时代》杂志工作了21年，主要关注苏美关系，曾任华盛顿分社社长和外交事务专栏作家。此后，他接到了刚刚当选的克林顿的电话。

塔尔博特于1994年加入美国国务院，很快升任副国务卿。在这一职位上，他是克林顿政府对俄及其他前苏联国家政策的制定者，并在1998年印度核试验后主持了美印之间的谈判。

“斯特罗布是一位善良而杰出的人，他让我们的世界更加和平与安全，”克林顿在塔尔博特去世后发表的一份声明中说。他说，塔尔博特在牛津翻译赫鲁晓夫回忆录时，每天为他做早餐是克林顿的任务，并补充道：“不知怎的，我占了便宜。”

他说，他和希拉里都对“一位了不起的朋友、一位世界级人物的离去”“深感悲痛”。

此后，他于2002年至2017年担任布鲁金斯学会主席。在此期间，他还主持了美国国务院外交事务政策委员会。

塔尔博特还著有十余本书。他的最后一本书名为《我们国父的警告：理性时代遇上特朗普时代》，于2020年出版。

他1946年出生于俄亥俄州代顿，身后留下两个儿子德文和阿德里安，以及六个孙辈。

他的第一任妻子布鲁克·希勒于2009年去世，他后来与作家芭芭拉·拉齐尔·阿舍结婚。

Could housing decide Spain's general election?

Could housing decide Spain's general election?

Housing has been the biggest issue for voters ahead of Spain's general election on Sunday, with millions of people protesting across the country in recent weeks over a lack of affordable homes.

Final opinion polls suggest the conservative People's Party will receive the most votes and that the right-wing Vox party is set to enter the national government for the first time. It would mean an end to Socialist prime minister Pedro Sánchez's eight years in power.

Europe correspondent Nick Beake speaks to a young couple from Valencia, who have been kept apart due to high rents in their city.

If Prime Minister Christopher Luxon cannot reach a deal to form a ruling coalition, New Zealand will have to hold fresh elections.

People enter a voting place at St Anne’s Anglican Church on the day of the general election in Wellington, New Zealand, Nov 7, 2026. (Photo: Reuters/Hollie Adams)

WELLINGTON: New Zealand’s ruling centre-right coalition has narrowly missed winning a parliamentary majority, final election results showed on Friday (Nov 27), leaving Prime Minister Christopher Luxon needing the support of the centrist Opportunity Party to remain in power.

WASHINGTON: US President Donald Trump said on Thursday (Nov 26) that he had seen sufficient information that Nvidia's Jensen Huang was not a security threat, while touting his administration's intervention to save the scandal-plagued CEO's job as "a great thing" for the world.

"I think he's absolutely fine," Trump told reporters at his Mar-a-Lago estate.

Asked by AFP how he could be sure when the Justice Department would not confirm it had conducted a thorough investigation into Huang, Trump said his belief was based on "information I have, which is a lot of information".

Huang, a key figure in the AI revolution, was forced to resign earlier this month after revelations that he had an affair with a business executive who reportedly has ties to Chinese intelligence and whose company may have helped China obtain advanced chips in violation of US export controls.

French actor Gerard Depardieu to face trial for rape, court rules

Gerard Depardieu has denied the allegations and could be jailed for up to 20 years if found guilty.

PARIS: Film star Gerard Depardieu, one of the leading faces of French cinema, will face trial on charges of raping actress Charlotte Arnould in 2018, after a Paris appeal court on Thursday (Nov 26) rejected his bid to avoid having the case tried.

Arnould first accused Depardieu of rape in 2018, saying the assaults occurred in his Paris home on two separate occasions when she was in her early 20s. Depardieu, 77, has denied wrongdoing in the case, and his legal team last year appealed the investigative judge's decision for the case to be tried.

However, the Paris appeals court upheld the decision for the case to be tried in criminal court. It ruled that Depardieu would be tried for allegedly raping Arnould on Aug 7 2018, but dismissed a second alleged rape on Aug 13 2018.

Earlier this month, Depardieu withdrew his appeal against a separate 2025 conviction for sexual assault, accepting his guilt and apologizing to his victims.

"She has been waiting for this moment for a long time," Durrieu Diebolt said. "She is fully prepared for it."

The appeals court said Depardieu could appeal to France's highest court, the Cour ​de Cassation. His lawyer, David-Olivier Kaminski, said they were waiting to see if they would do so.

Nearly 200,000 homes and businesses had no power in Virginia and another 177,000 in Maryland as of 2:26pm ET (Friday, 3.26am, Singapore time) according to poweroutage.us, which also showed Pennsylvania, New Jersey and North Carolina each had tens of thousands of utility customers without electricity.

items.title: Albania's youth are protesting, no longer leaving the country
items.summary: Youth protests against a rigid political system and corruption have shaken the government of Albanian Prime Minister Edi Rama. They also show that fewer young people are willing to emigrate in search of a better future.
items.body:
https://p.dw.com/p/5PxaV

Prefer DW on Google

Most of the 'Flamingo Revolution' protests in Albania have been peaceful Image: Vlasov Sulaj/NurPhoto/picture alliance

Advertisement

In mid-October, students in the Albanian capital Tirana set a suitcase on fire and threw it into the courtyard of the Education Ministry. Everyone in the country understood the symbolism: According to the 2023 census, the population of this Western Balkan country shrunk by about 420,000 between 2011 and 2023 — by nearly 15% — primarily because of emigration.

For a generation of young Albanians, this was the response to a system that gave them little voice. But now young people want to stay, and the protesters are saying that the system has to change.

Known as the "Flamingo Revolution," the social movement began in May with demonstrations against a luxury resort in a coastal reserve that US President Donald Trump's daughter Ivanka Trump and her husband Jared Kushner were involved in.

It quickly evolved into broader criticism against corruption, Prime Minister Edi Rama's government and his ruling Socialist Party and the country's entire political class.

Thousands marched almost every evening for four months in protests that were largely peaceful. But on October 13, a student protest escalated and there were clashes with police. Since then, the unrest has continued, with police using tear gas, water cannons and rubber bullets against demonstrators. There have been hundreds of arrests and many injuries, amid damage to public and private property.

'Flamingo revolution' has broad support

The protesters have called for Rama's resignation, a transitional government, electoral reform and fresh elections. The movement, which has no leader, has support from people across the political spectrum. And while the prime minister has blamed "foreign hands" for the movement, there seems to be little evidence that external actors are orchestrating the protests, though they may have attempted to exploit the unrest online.

The protesters, who do not feel represented by Albania's democracy, are driven by domestic issues: corruption, the high cost of living and low wages. This is nothing new, but many factors have converged recently: a series of high-level corruption charges, including against ministers and two of Rama's former deputies, rising prices and the fact that Albania is being measured against EU standards by a new generation.

In certain areas, Rama has transformed Albania since taking office in 2013: the economy has grown significantly, as the government likes to point out, and tourism is booming. But the prosperity remains unevenly distributed. Critics accuse the government of channeling too much taxpayer money into a small number of well-connected companies through prestigious projects and public-private partnerships, and in some cases through corrupt business deals, at the expense of healthcare, education and better economic prospects for the wider population.

Rama has rejected the calls for his resignation and has invited protesters to engage in dialogue, which they have so far refused.

Clashes with police erupted in mid-October like here in TiranaImage: Adnan Beci/AFP

Alternating between Socialist and Democratic Party

In 2008, Rama and Sali Berisha, the long-time chairman of the opposition Democratic Party, worked on a reform to Albania's constitution and electoral law, which was approved by parliament. Since then, it is party leaders who have determined who enters Parliament, which weakens ties between lawmakers and their constituents.

In addition, it has become significantly more difficult for new parties to win seats. In 2025, a new party received about 64,000 votes, but only one seat. The Socialists, by contrast, won about one seat for every 10,000 votes.

Rama has been the leader of the Socialists since 2005, while Berisha first became the chairman of the Democratic Party in 1991. For 21 years, Albania's prime minister has either been Rama or Berisha. Freedom House, a US nongovernmental organization that promotes democracy worldwide, classifies Albania as "partly free" and describes the country's political parties as being "often organized around leading personalities."

Protesters on the streets have said that they want both men to be jailed. Rama has argued that governments should be replaced at the ballot box, not on the streets.

Though the Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe (OSCE) acknowledged that parliamentary elections in 2025 were "competitive and professionally managed" it said that they had taken place "in a highly polarized environment and contestants did not enjoy a level playing field."

It added that there were "reports of intimidation, misuse of public resources and pressure on public employees, which undermined equal opportunities."

The Democratic Party also spoke of election fraud and intimidation. Turnout was below 45%.

Protesters call out corruption, face high cost of living

Many protesters also allege that when it comes to business, what matters is the proximity to people in power. They criticize the public procurement, public auctions and concessions system, which has led to state-owned land, including coastal and protected areas, being sold to private investors.

Ordinary Albanians are feeling the financial brunt. According to the Albanian Institute of Statistics (INSTAT), half of all employees earn less than 60,000 lek (roughly €620 or $680) per month after taxes. But according to Eurostat, food prices are slightly above the EU average and real estate prices in Tirana have nearly doubled since 2018, with rents rising just as quickly.

For many years, young Albanians who were dissatisfied with the system opted to leave the country. The number of Albanian citizens in Germany more than doubled between 2018 and 2024, reaching almost 120,000.

Though it is still too early to say whether there are fewer Albanians leaving today, for many protesters staying has become a political statement.

Albanians continue to call for the prime minister's resignationImage: Florion Goga/REUTERS

Albanians largely pro-EU

Rama has argued that his resignation would jeopardize Albania's bid to join the European Union by 2030, but the vast majority of Albanians are pro-European, including those on the streets and in the opposition. From the protesters' perspective, it is the government headed by Rama that is the real obstacle on the path to the EU.

Though there is currently a wave of protests across Europe, the only obvious comparison is with Serbia, where a student-led movement recently forced a long-time ruler from office. Whether Albania will follow this example depends on whether young people, who have traditionally not been deeply engaged in politics, can turn their protests into votes.

What is certain is that for three decades, Albania's leaders have relied on their citizens' suitcases. Now, the country's students have burned that very luggage.

Andi Balla is a doctoral candidate at the Leibniz Institute for East and Southeast European Studies (IOS) in Regensburg, where he is conducting research on demographic debates in Albania. He has written numerous articles on Albania for an international audience.

translation.summary: 针对僵化政治体制和腐败的青年抗议震动了阿尔巴尼亚总理埃迪·拉马的政府。这些抗议也表明，愿意为寻求更好未来而移民的年轻人越来越少。

translation.body:
https://p.dw.com/p/5PxaV

在谷歌上首选德国之声

阿尔巴尼亚大多数“火烈鸟革命”抗议活动都是和平的 图片：Vlasov Sulaj/NurPhoto/picture alliance

广告

10月中旬，阿尔巴尼亚首都地拉那的学生点燃了一个手提箱，并将其扔进教育部庭院。全国上下都明白这一象征意义：根据2023年人口普查，这个西巴尔干国家的人口在2011年至2023年间减少了约42万——近15%——主要原因是移民。

对一代阿尔巴尼亚年轻人来说，这是对一个几乎不给他们发言权的体制的回应。但现在年轻人想留下来，抗议者表示体制必须改变。

这场被称为“火烈鸟革命”的社会运动始于5月，当时示威活动反对一座位于海岸保护区的豪华度假村，美国总统唐纳德·特朗普的女儿伊万卡·特朗普及其丈夫贾里德·库什纳参与其中。

它很快演变为对腐败、总理埃迪·拉马政府及其执政的社会党以及该国整个政治阶层的更广泛批评。

四个月来，数千人几乎每晚都举行游行，抗议活动基本和平。但10月13日，一场学生抗议升级，与警察发生冲突。此后，骚乱持续不断，警察对示威者使用催泪瓦斯、水炮和橡皮子弹。已有数百人被捕，多人受伤，公共和私人财产遭到破坏。

“火烈鸟革命”获得广泛支持

抗议者呼吁拉马辞职、组建过渡政府、进行选举改革并举行新的选举。这场没有领导人的运动得到了各政治派别人士的支持。尽管总理将这场运动归咎于“外国之手”，但似乎几乎没有证据表明有外部行为者在策划抗议，不过他们可能试图在网上利用骚乱。

抗议者感到阿尔巴尼亚的民主没有代表他们，他们被国内问题所驱动：腐败、高昂的生活成本和低工资。这并非新鲜事，但许多因素最近汇聚在一起：一系列高层腐败指控，包括针对部长和拉马的两名前副手的指控，物价上涨，以及新一代人正以欧盟标准来衡量阿尔巴尼亚。

在某些领域，拉马自2013年上任以来改变了阿尔巴尼亚：经济显著增长，政府喜欢指出这一点，旅游业蓬勃发展。但繁荣仍然分配不均。批评者指责政府通过声望项目和公私合作伙伴关系，在某些情况下通过腐败的商业交易，将过多纳税人的钱输送给少数关系密切的公司，牺牲了医疗、教育和更广泛民众更好的经济前景。

拉马拒绝了辞职的呼吁，并邀请抗议者进行对话，但迄今为止他们拒绝了。

10月中旬在地拉那等地爆发了与警察的冲突 图片：Adnan Beci/AFP

在社会党与民主党之间交替

2008年，拉马和反对党民主党长期主席萨利·贝里沙共同推动了一项对阿尔巴尼亚宪法和选举法的改革，并获得议会批准。此后，由政党领导人决定谁进入议会，这削弱了议员与其选民之间的联系。

此外，新政党赢得席位的难度显著增加。2025年，一个新政党获得约6.4万张选票，但只赢得一个席位。相比之下，社会党大约每1万张选票赢得一个席位。

拉马自2005年以来一直是社会党领导人，而贝里沙于1991年首次成为民主党主席。21年来，阿尔巴尼亚的总理不是拉马就是贝里沙。自由之家，一个在全球推广民主的美国非政府组织，将阿尔巴尼亚列为“部分自由”，并称该国的政党“往往围绕主要人物组织”。

街头抗议者表示，他们希望两人都被监禁。拉马则主张政府应在投票箱而非街头被替换。

尽管欧洲安全与合作组织（OSCE）承认2025年的议会选举“具有竞争性且管理专业”，但表示选举发生在“高度两极化的环境中，竞争者没有享有公平的竞争环境”。

它还补充说，“有报道称存在恐吓、滥用公共资源和对公职人员的施压，这破坏了平等机会。”

民主党也谈到了选举舞弊和恐吓。投票率低于45%。

抗议者揭露腐败，面临高昂生活成本

许多抗议者还声称，在商业方面，重要的是与掌权者的关系。他们批评公共采购、公开拍卖和特许权制度，这导致国有土地，包括沿海和保护区的土地，被出售给私人投资者。

普通阿尔巴尼亚人正感受到经济压力。根据阿尔巴尼亚统计研究所（INSTAT）的数据，一半雇员的税后月收入低于6万列克（约620欧元或680美元）。但根据欧盟统计局的数据，食品价格略高于欧盟平均水平，地拉那的房地产价格自2018年以来几乎翻了一番，租金上涨速度同样快。

多年来，对体制不满的年轻阿尔巴尼亚人选择离开该国。2018年至2024年间，在德国的阿尔巴尼亚公民人数增加了一倍多，达到近12万人。

尽管现在说离开的阿尔巴尼亚人是否减少还为时过早，但对许多抗议者来说，留下来已成为一种政治表态。

阿尔巴尼亚人继续呼吁总理辞职 图片：Florion Goga/REUTERS

阿尔巴尼亚人总体上支持加入欧盟

拉马主张，他的辞职将危及阿尔巴尼亚到2030年加入欧盟的努力，但绝大多数阿尔巴尼亚人支持欧洲，包括街头抗议者和反对派。从抗议者的角度来看，拉马领导的政府才是通往欧盟道路上的真正障碍。

尽管目前欧洲各地出现抗议浪潮，但唯一明显的比较是塞尔维亚，那里一场由学生领导的运动最近迫使一位长期统治者下台。阿尔巴尼亚是否会效仿这一榜样，取决于传统上并未深度参与政治的年轻人能否将抗议转化为选票。

可以肯定的是，三十年来，阿尔巴尼亚的领导人一直依赖其公民的手提箱。现在，该国的学生烧毁了那件行李。

安迪·巴拉是雷根斯堡莱布尼茨东欧和东南欧研究研究所（IOS）的博士候选人，他在那里研究阿尔巴尼亚的人口辩论。他为国际读者撰写了大量关于阿尔巴尼亚的文章。

本文译自德语。

Crew member dies after diesel tanker capsizes off Ibiza, no pollution so far

The tanker carried up to 7,000 tonnes of diesel, but authorities reported no major spill and activated Spain’s Level 2 maritime pollution response plan.

A rescue vessel moves next to the capsized oil tanker Med Emre off Ibiza, Spain, Nov 26, 2026. (Photo: REUTERS/CGT Mar y Puertos)

MADRID: At least one crew member aboard a ship carrying diesel has died after the vessel capsized and partially sank off the Spanish island of Ibiza on Thursday (Nov 26), regional authorities said, adding there were no signs of pollution so far.

The Malta-flagged chemical tanker Med Emre was sailing from Algeciras to Barcelona and may have been carrying up to 7,000 metric tons of diesel when it keeled over about 30 nautical miles (56 km) off Ibiza's northwestern coast, the Balearic Islands' interior department said.

Emergency services said all 17 crew members were rescued, but one died after being taken directly to Ibiza's Can Misses hospital. Six others were brought to Ibiza airport and taken to two hospitals with light injuries, primarily hypothermia.

Of the remaining crew, five were taken to Valencia and five remained in good condition aboard a rescue vessel, they added.

Pablo Garriz, the Balearic Islands' regional head of emergencies, said the crew included Turkish and Indian nationals, but he could not yet confirm the nationality of the deceased.

The tanker remained partially submerged with its keel protruding above the surface, Garriz told reporters, despite initial indications that it had sunk completely.

"The positive news is that the vessel is not on the seabed but remains semi-submerged at the surface, which allows salvage and containment operations," he said, adding there was currently no impact on Balearic waters or coastline and no evidence of a significant spill, although small sheens had been observed.

Technical experts were assessing the vessel's stability before deciding on salvage and cargo-recovery operations, he added.

Spain's maritime rescue service sent an aircraft and a vessel specialised in oil-spill response, the Clara Campoamor, to survey the area. Three helicopters took part in the rescue, along with nearby merchant vessels.

Spain's merchant marine authority activated the national maritime pollution contingency plan at level 2, the second-highest.

The waters surrounding Ibiza are a habitat for sea turtles, dolphins and the Balearic shearwater, one of Europe's most threatened seabirds. The area is also home to extensive meadows of Posidonia oceanica seagrass, which plays a vital role in supporting marine biodiversity.

Spain's worst maritime environmental disaster occurred in 2002, when the Bahamas-flagged tanker Prestige sank off the northwestern Galicia region, spilling tens of thousands of tons of heavy fuel oil and fouling hundreds of beaches in Spain and France.

The Balearic regional government said it was gathering information on the accident and its possible consequences, including any risk of fuel pollution, before deciding on further measures.

RIYADH: The Saudi-led military coalition fighting Yemen's Houthis said on Thursday (Nov 26) that the Iran-aligned group had attacked Saudi Aramco's Jazan refinery, a day after hitting the largest oil refinery in the kingdom.

The refinery in the southwestern city of Jazan, near the Yemeni border, is designed to process up to 400,000 barrels of crude oil per day.

The coalition said it had later destroyed a ballistic missile launch platform in the Yemeni port city of Hodeidah, which it said the Houthis had used in Thursday's attack on the refinery.

items.title: Saudi pop music is thriving — but for the right reasons?
items.summary: As part of Vision 2030, Saudi Arabia's music scene has evolved hugely thanks to state funding and support. Local musicians and DJs are optimistic. But are they actually just helping prop up an authoritarian state?
items.body:
https://p.dw.com/p/5Pp1R

Prefer DW on Google

Although there are no pictures of state figureheads at big Saudi events, attendees say they know the state funds festivals and they suspect plainclothes security staff monitor the crowd Image: Fayez Nureldine/AFP

Advertisement

Today, rapper Asayel Bishi is one of Saudi Arabia's rising hip-hop stars, signed to the country's biggest record label for new music, MDLBEAST. But not so long ago, she was making international headlines for a totally different reason.

In 2020, after Bishi released a music video for a song, "Bint Mecca," or "girl from Mecca," featuring people dancing in a local cafe, Mecca's governor called for the arrest of Bishi's whole production team. He said the video violated the holy city's local customs and traditions. In the end, the situation was resolved with a discussion about filming permits.

And by early 2023, Bishi was signed to MDLBEAST and has since racked up hundreds of thousands of streams on music platforms like Spotify.

In the past, other Saudi rappers have ended up in prison for similar, alleged transgressions. The fact that Bishi's story went a different way is probably partially because the 31-year-old's career path is on a similar trajectory to the Saudi pop music industry as a whole.

Music part of Vision 2030

As part of Saudi ruler Mohammed bin Salman's Vision 2030 plan, announced in 2016 and which aims to move the country away from economic dependence on oil, the country has poured billions into the local music industry.

The pace of development increased in 2019 after the country held its first major festival, Soundstorm, an annual event that now draws major international acts and over 400,000 guests. MDLBEAST was created then, primarily as the festival organizer. Since then, it has also become a record label, radio station, distributor, promoter and talent incubator.

After decades of bans on concerts, the first officially sanctioned music gigs began to be held in 2017. Here, visitors arrive at the Soundstorm music festival in Banban in December 2025Image: Fayez Nureldine/AFP

A recent report for the Saudi Music Commission suggests the music sector could be worth $500 million (€455 million) by 2034. But it's difficult to figure out how well Saudi pop is really doing now because independent monitoring of the sector only began relatively recently.

Streaming platform Spotify reports that people listening to Saudi-made music inside Saudi Arabia increased by 195% between 2020 and 2024. However, the most-streamed artists inside the country are still international.

'Tied to the destiny of crown prince'

Although there was a mostly-hidden Saudi music scene before this recent boom, observers say the growth of the Saudi music sector is not organic.

It's all about building an industry from the top down, Amr Abdelrahim, a researcher at Sciences Po in Paris, reported in a 2024 study. "After 2016, young middle-class musicians and creative professionals, who had been careful to avoid drawing official attention to their countercultural activities suddenly became central to the ambitions of the state," he wrote.

The careers of young Saudi acts — like Bishi, for example — "became tied to the destiny of the crown prince," the researcher explained.

The Saudi royal family has long dispersed money from Saudi oil sales to their subjects, in order to ensure economic dependence and loyalty. But, Abdelrahim argued, "what is new about Saudi investments in culture under MBS is an unprecedented degree of centralization and the emergence of new clientelist networks around the country's de-facto ruler," using a common abbreviation for Crown Prince Mohammed.

Those involved "are inadvertently participating in the consolidation of the Saudi regime," he argued.

Observers have noted the level of control around musical events in Saudi Arabia, with one researcher saying she was unable to find video evidence of bad behavior later, even though many visitors had filmed itImage: Fayez Nureldine/AFP

Observers say a lot of the new music businesses are vague about their ties to the state. But it's clear they couldn't work without the state's financial support and approval.

"Almost all major events are organized by the state or funded by closely linked entities," a spokesperson from Saudi-focused organization, ALQST for Human Rights, told DW. "This affects the type of music produced, as musicians have to be mindful of what is acceptable. This is not just about the music they produce, but also how they act and what they say to their fans."

ALQST believes Saudi musicians have even less artistic freedom under the new musical system than before, when they would have played or performed privately. They can lose their contracts and livelihoods, be prevented from performing or even arrested, ALQST's spokesperson said.

Hidden for two decades

"In the past, the music scene was not regulated," explained the guitarist and bassist for Saudi black metal band, Al-Namrood. But now that it is, the state can more closely monitor musicians who once stayed hidden and only played privately, the musician, who goes by the name of Mephisto, told DW.

Al-Namrood are one of the rare examples of a Saudi act that isn't working with state support. The group first formed in 2008 but have never played at home and have kept their identities secret for almost two decades.

"The exchange is clear: You want to perform, it has to be under our rules," Mephisto continued. "And I totally understand the perspective [of some musicians]. But typically the artist must refrain from any criticism of the religious or authoritarian. [The state] doesn't necessarily buy an artist's loyalty, it just creates incentives that make criticism increasingly costly."

For Al-Namrood, who have often condemned Saudi conservatism, religion and politics in their music, that's not an option. "We don't want anything to do with them," Mephisto said.

In her 2020 paper for the journal, Arabian Humanities, Nora Derbal, a professor at the University of Hamburg, said Saudi artists told her that if they got a call from authorities asking them to participate in a government project, it would be an offer they couldn't turn down.

The artists she spoke with were debating "their cooptation and loss of autonomy, and about the consequences for not joining in state projects," she wrote.

On the other hand, in various interviews, Saudi acts who have partaken in their country's pop music renaissance have also been positive: They don't have to hide anymore, they can play for larger audiences and they are paid. In an interview, one Saudi DJ described the first Soundstorm festival as like "Berlin after the fall of the wall" while others said they felt they were making history.

"So that's the interesting paradox," said Fannie Agerschou-Madsen, a postdoctoral researcher at the University of Roskilde in Denmark, who's written several papers on the topic. "We have all these social liberalizations and challenges to conservative norms but at the same time that's not being followed by political liberalization."

Before 2016, DJs only performed in private homes, compounds or beach resorts. One Saudi DJ described Soundstorm, seen here in 2022, as 'kind of our Woodstock'Image: Fayez Nureldine/AFP

Is the state co-opting local musicians?

But that doesn't mean that some room isn't being created for meaningful change, Agerschou-Madsen told DW. Locals told her they enjoyed the newfound freedom of going to a dance party although, she noted, the subversiveness seemed to be more directed at the social conservatism than Saudi authorities.

Young Saudis are well aware of the red lines and state control of the music scene and are continually negotiating boundaries, the researcher argued. In that way, "their everyday practices create space for political and social change, little by little, although perhaps not in what you'd consider a typically revolutionary way."

So is the Saudi state co-opting local musicians, including those who might have said something controversial before they ever get a chance to?

A DW enquiry to MDLBEAST was not answered. And the answer likely lies somewhere in the middle.

For some young Saudis, the new music scene has been about fun, self-expression, belonging and creativity, Agerschou-Madsen wrote in a new, as-yet-unpublished paper shared with DW. blocks.text: Although there are no pictures of state figureheads at big Saudi events, attendees say they know the state funds festivals and they suspect plainclothes security staff monitor the crowd Image: Fayez Nureldine/AFP

Today, rapper Asayel Bishi is one of Saudi Arabia's rising hip-hop stars, signed to the country's biggest record label for new music, MDLBEAST. But not so long ago, she was making international headlines for a totally different reason.

In 2020, after Bishi released a music video for a song, "Bint Mecca," or "girl from Mecca," featuring people dancing in a local cafe, Mecca's governor called for the arrest of Bishi's whole production team. He said the video violated the holy city's local customs and traditions. In the end, the situation was resolved with a discussion about filming permits.
And by early 2023, Bishi was signed to MDLBEAST and has since racked up hundreds of thousands of streams on music platforms like Spotify.

In the past, other Saudi rappers have ended up in prison for similar, alleged transgressions. The fact that Bishi's story went a different way is probably partially because the 31-year-old's career path is on a similar trajectory to the Saudi pop music industry as a whole.
Music part of Vision 2030

As part of Saudi ruler Mohammed bin Salman's Vision 2030 plan, announced in 2016 and which aims to move the country away from economic dependence on oil, the country has poured billions into the local music industry.

The pace of development increased in 2019 after the country held its first major festival, Soundstorm, an annual event that now draws major international acts and over 400,000 guests. MDLBEAST was created then, primarily as the festival organizer. Since then, it has also become a record label, radio station, distributor, promoter and talent incubator.

After decades of bans on concerts, the first officially sanctioned music gigs began to be held in 2017. Here, visitors arrive at the Soundstorm music festival in Banban in December 2025Image: Fayez Nureldine/AFP

A recent report for the Saudi Music Commission suggests the music sector could be worth $500 million (€455 million) by 2034. But it's difficult to figure out how well Saudi pop is really doing now because independent monitoring of the sector only began relatively recently.

Streaming platform Spotify reports that people listening to Saudi-made music inside Saudi Arabia increased by 195% between 2020 and 2024. However, the most-streamed artists inside the country are still international.
'Tied to the destiny of crown prince'
Although there was a mostly-hidden Saudi music scene before this recent boom, observers say the growth of the Saudi music sector is not organic.

It's all about building an industry from the top down, Amr Abdelrahim, a researcher at Sciences Po in Paris, reported in a 2024 study. "After 2016, young middle-class musicians and creative professionals, who had been careful to avoid drawing official attention to their countercultural activities suddenly became central to the ambitions of the state," he wrote.
The careers of young Saudi acts — like Bishi, for example — "became tied to the destiny of the crown prince," the researcher explained.

The Saudi royal family has long dispersed money from Saudi oil sales to their subjects, in order to ensure economic dependence and loyalty. But, Abdelrahim argued, "what is new about Saudi investments in culture under MBS is an unprecedented degree of centralization and the emergence of new clientelist networks around the country's de-facto ruler," using a common abbreviation for Crown Prince Mohammed.
Those involved "are inadvertently participating in the consolidation of the Saudi regime," he argued.

Observers have noted the level of control around musical events in Saudi Arabia, with one researcher saying she was unable to find video evidence of bad behavior later, even though many visitors had filmed itImage: Fayez Nureldine/AFP
Observers say a lot of the new music businesses are vague about their ties to the state. But it's clear they couldn't work without the state's financial support and approval.

"Almost all major events are organized by the state or funded by closely linked entities," a spokesperson from Saudi-focused organization, ALQST for Human Rights, told DW. "This affects the type of music produced, as musicians have to be mindful of what is acceptable. This is not just about the music they produce, but also how they act and what they say to their fans."

ALQST believes Saudi musicians have even less artistic freedom under the new musical system than before, when they would have played or performed privately. They can lose their contracts and livelihoods, be prevented from performing or even arrested, ALQST's spokesperson said.
Hidden for two decades

"In the past, the music scene was not regulated," explained the guitarist and bassist for Saudi black metal band, Al-Namrood. But now that it is, the state can more closely monitor musicians who once stayed hidden and only played privately, the musician, who goes by the name of Mephisto, told DW.

Al-Namrood are one of the rare examples of a Saudi act that isn't working with state support. The group first formed in 2008 but have never played at home and have kept their identities secret for almost two decades.

"The exchange is clear: You want to perform, it has to be under our rules," Mephisto continued. "And I totally understand the perspective [of some musicians]. But typically the artist must refrain from any criticism of the religious or authoritarian. [The state] doesn't necessarily buy an artist's loyalty, it just creates incentives that make criticism increasingly costly."
For Al-Namrood, who have often condemned Saudi conservatism, religion and politics in their music, that's not an option. "We don't want anything to do with them," Mephisto said.

In her 2020 paper for the journal, Arabian Humanities, Nora Derbal, a professor at the University of Hamburg, said Saudi artists told her that if they got a call from authorities asking them to participate in a government project, it would be an offer they couldn't turn down.
The artists she spoke with were debating "their cooptation and loss of autonomy, and about the consequences for not joining in state projects," she wrote.

On the other hand, in various interviews, Saudi acts who have partaken in their country's pop music renaissance have also been positive: They don't have to hide anymore, they can play for larger audiences and they are paid. In an interview, one Saudi DJ described the first Soundstorm festival as like "Berlin after the fall of the wall" while others said they felt they were making history.

"So that's the interesting paradox," said Fannie Agerschou-Madsen, a postdoctoral researcher at the University of Roskilde in Denmark, who's written several papers on the topic. "We have all these social liberalizations and challenges to conservative norms but at the same time that's not being followed by political liberalization."
Before 2016, DJs only performed in private homes, compounds or beach resorts. One Saudi DJ described Soundstorm, seen here in 2022, as 'kind of our Woodstock'Image: Fayez Nureldine/AFP

But that doesn't mean that some room isn't being created for meaningful change, Agerschou-Madsen told DW. Locals told her they enjoyed the newfound freedom of going to a dance party although, she noted, the subversiveness seemed to be more directed at the social conservatism than Saudi authorities.

Young Saudis are well aware of the red lines and state control of the music scene and are continually negotiating boundaries, the researcher argued. In that way, "their everyday practices create space for political and social change, little by little, although perhaps not in what you'd consider a typically revolutionary way."
So is the Saudi state co-opting local musicians, including those who might have said something controversial before they ever get a chance to?
A DW enquiry to MDLBEAST was not answered. And the answer likely lies somewhere in the middle.

For some young Saudis, the new music scene has been about fun, self-expression, belonging and creativity, Agerschou-Madsen wrote in a new, as-yet-unpublished paper shared with DW. "Others, however, view it as a top-down project that commodifies fun while sidestepping deeper issues of political freedom and social equity."

items.title: Congo Ebola outbreak reaches 12,000 cases as some responders evacuate
items.summary: As the fast-moving outbreak continues to spread in eastern Congo, fighting between rebels and the army is disrupting efforts to contain the spread of the disease.
items.body:
World

Congo Ebola outbreak reaches 12,000 cases as some responders evacuate

November 26, 20268:47 AM ET

By

The Associated Press

Relatives and healthcare workers prepare to bury a victim of Ebola, in Beni, North Kivu province, Congo, Tuesday, Nov. 24, 2026.

Sebastien Kitsa Musayi/AP

hide caption

Sebastien Kitsa Musayi/AP

BUNIA, Congo (AP) — The fast-moving Ebola outbreak in eastern Congo has topped 12,000 confirmed cases, government data showed Thursday, as fighting between rebels and the army disrupts efforts to contain the spread of the disease.

It is the fastest-growing Ebola outbreak in history and nearly half the 12,021 people confirmed to have the virus have died, according to data from Congo's Ministry of Health. It is also the deadliest of Congo's 17 outbreaks and is on track to surpass the death toll from the West African outbreak that killed 11,000 people between 2014 and 2016.

The outbreak declared in May is caused by the rare Bundibugyo virus, for which there is no approved vaccine or treatment. Response teams are battling armed conflict, poor roads and violence from residents fueled by mistrust and misinformation.

Ebola spreads through direct contact with the blood or other bodily fluids of people who are sick or have died from the disease. Containing the disease requires quickly identifying and treating patients in isolation, monitoring people who may have been exposed and safely burying the dead.

Fighting between the army and the Convention pour la révolution populaire rebels resumed Thursday morning in Iga-Barrière, a mining town about 25 kilometers (15 miles) north of Bunia in eastern Congo, sending new waves of displaced people toward the city. Bunia is the capital of northeastern Ituri province and a major hub for the Ebola response.

CRP is one of more than 100 armed groups in eastern Congo, where conflict has created one of the world's most severe humanitarian crises. The group was founded last year by former warlord Thomas Lubanga, who was convicted by the International Criminal Court in 2012 of recruiting children under 15 and using them in fighting.

Fighting between the army and the rebels earlier this week had already prevented teams from reaching some communities, disrupted monitoring of people exposed to the virus and left some treatment centers with fewer staff, Dr. Catherine Smallwood, the World Health Organization's Ebola incident manager, said Wednesday.

Smallwood said that about a dozen people, including two WHO personnel and Congolese health officials, were evacuated to Bunia on Tuesday after three full days trapped in a hospital in Akwe, northeast of the provincial capital, amid intense crossfire.

items.title: North Korea's Kim vows to build more nuclear weapons after ignoring Trump's overture
items.summary: Leader Kim Jong Un reportedly visited facilities that produce nuclear ingredients and called for building more nuclear weapons to cope with threats from the U.S. and South Korea.
items.body:
World

North Korea's Kim vows to build more nuclear weapons after ignoring Trump's overture

November 26, 20268:31 AM ET

By

The Associated Press

In this photo provided by the North Korean government, leader Kim Jong Un inspects a facility the government says is for producing weapons-grade nuclear material at an undisclosed location in North Korea, Monday, Nov. 25, 2026.

Korean Central News Agency/Korea News Service via AP

hide caption

Korean Central News Agency/Korea News Service via AP

SEOUL, South Korea (AP) — North Korean leader Kim Jong Un visited facilities that produce nuclear ingredients and called for building more nuclear weapons, days after ignoring U.S. President Donald Trump's offer to meet during his recent visit to Asia.

Experts say Kim likely wants to show off his evolving nuclear arsenal, the backbone of his authoritarian rule, and reaffirm his rejection of any future talks on dismantling his nuclear program.

The North's official Korean Central News Agency said Thursday that Kim inspected two nuclear materials production factories, one newly inaugurated and the other being expanded. KCNA photos showed Kim and senior military officials walking between dense rows of what appeared to be centrifuges used to produce weapons-grade uranium and touring halls displaying what were believed to be warheads. Some of the images were blurred.

KCNA said Kim visited a nuclear-powered equipment production base and a nuclear research institute as well on Wednesday.

North Korea has disclosed a uranium enrichment site a few times since it showed one at its main Yongbyon nuclear complex to visiting American scholars in 2010. North Korea didn't say where the nuclear materials production factories that Kim visited this week are located. In June, when North Korea disclosed parts of a uranium enrichment site while reporting on Kim's visit there, outside experts assessed it was likely an additional uranium enrichment facility at Yongbyon.

Kim justifies nuke program by citing threats from US, South KoreaKim said his latest inspection visit was part of efforts to strengthen North Korea's defense capabilities in response to "variable nuclear threats approaching the Korean Peninsula moment by moment." He accused the U.S. of inciting its regional allies to possess nuclear-powered submarines and committing to sharing its nuclear weapons with them, KCNA said.

"The validity and substantiality of our possession of nuclear weapons and the trend of bolstering up its nuclear capability in quality and quantity are an irreversible reality," Kim said, according to KCNA.

Kim also said the deployment of low-yield battlefield nuclear weapons across multiple domains for various missions is crucial and urgent given North Korea's "inevitable reality facing the border with the most dangerous enemy state," a reference to South Korea. North Korea has in recent years focused on developing such tactical nuclear weapons amid heightened animosity with South Korea.

"Trump has talked about a willingness to meet Kim Jong Un, but the basic U.S. position that North Korea must denuclearize remains unchanged. So Kim Jong Un wants to say 'Look at how powerful we are. Don't talk about denuclearization if you want to meet us,'" said Moon Seong Mook, an analyst for the Seoul-based Korea Research Institute for National Strategy.

Moon said Kim's visit to the nuclear facilities was also likely meant to check on how state objectives on the nuclear program have progressed this year and what future goals must be set ahead of a year-end Workers' Party conference.

South Korea's Defense Ministry said it takes Kim's comments on battlefield nuclear weapons seriously and added that Seoul maintains a firm military readiness against Pyongyang's nuclear threats under an alliance with the U.S. South Korea's Joint Chiefs of Staff declined to share an analysis of the North Korean nuclear facilities reported by KCNA, calling it confidential information for South Korea and the U.S.

Trump still hopes to meet KimTrump reiterated his eagerness to restore diplomacy with Kim as he visited China last week for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit. But a Trump-Kim meeting didn't happen, with Pyongyang not publicly responding to Trump's overture.

In an interview with the New York Post this week, Trump dismissed the suggestion that Kim had rebuffed his outreach, saying, "No, he didn't ignore it. You know, we had many leaders there … There'll be a time when we meet … It was just not really the right time. It was a very busy two-day period."

Trump also claimed he could revive diplomacy with Kim at any time by restarting the exchange of letters they maintained during his first term, although he acknowledged that the two leaders had not corresponded "recently."

Kim has previously said he could return to talks if the U.S. drops its "hostile policy" against his country and respects what he calls the North's status as a nuclear state. Experts say Kim aims to win international recognition as a nuclear state so that he could demand the lifting of international sanctions.

Last week, International Atomic Energy Agency Director General Rafael Grossi assessed North Korea has been expanding its original uranium enrichment facility at Yongbyon, calling the move "a cause for serious concern."

Nuclear weapons can be built using either highly enriched uranium or weapons-grade plutonium, and North Korea has facilities to produce both at Yongbyon. Last year, South Korea's Unification Minister Chung Dong-young said that North Korea was operating four uranium enrichment facilities and that they were running every day.

translation.body:
世界

朝鲜金正恩无视特朗普的会面提议后誓言建造更多核武器

2026年11月26日 上午8:31 东部时间

作者

美联社

在这张朝鲜政府提供的照片中，领导人金正恩于2026年11月25日星期一在朝鲜一处未公开地点视察政府所称用于生产武器级核材料的设施。

朝鲜中央通讯社/朝鲜新闻社 via 美联社

隐藏图注

朝鲜中央通讯社/朝鲜新闻社 via 美联社

韩国首尔（美联社）——朝鲜领导人金正恩视察了生产核原料的设施，并呼吁建造更多核武器。几天前，他无视了美国总统唐纳德·特朗普在最近访问亚洲期间提出的会面提议。

专家表示，金正恩很可能想展示其不断发展的核武库——这是他威权统治的支柱——并重申他拒绝未来就拆除其核计划进行任何谈判。

朝鲜官方媒体朝鲜中央通讯社周四表示，金正恩视察了两家核材料生产工厂，其中一家新近落成，另一家正在扩建。朝中社照片显示，金正恩和高级军事官员走在密集排列的、看似用于生产武器级铀的离心机之间，并参观了展示据信为弹头的展厅。部分图像被模糊处理。

朝中社称，金正恩周三还视察了一个核动力设备生产基地和一个核研究所。

自2010年向到访的美国学者展示其主要宁边核综合设施的一处铀浓缩设施以来，朝鲜已数次公开铀浓缩设施。朝鲜没有说明金正恩本周视察的核材料生产工厂位于何处。今年6月，朝鲜在报道金正恩视察时公开了一处铀浓缩设施的部分内容，外部专家评估那很可能是宁边的一处额外铀浓缩设施。

金正恩以美国和韩国的威胁为由为核计划辩护。金正恩表示，他最近的视察是其加强朝鲜防御能力努力的一部分，以应对“时刻逼近朝鲜半岛的变幻莫测的核威胁”。据朝中社报道，他指责美国煽动其地区盟友拥有核动力潜艇，并承诺与其分享核武器。

据朝中社报道，金正恩说：“我们拥有核武器的正当性和实质性，以及我们在质量和数量上加强核能力的趋势，是不可逆转的现实。”

金正恩还表示，鉴于朝鲜“面临与最危险敌对国家接壤的不可避免的现实”——指的是韩国——在多个领域部署用于各种任务的低当量战场核武器至关重要且紧迫。近年来，随着与韩国敌意加剧，朝鲜一直专注于发展此类战术核武器。

“特朗普谈到了愿意与金正恩会面，但美国要求朝鲜无核化的基本立场没有改变。所以金正恩想说‘看看我们有多强大。如果想见我们，就别谈无核化’，”首尔韩国国家战略研究院分析师文成默说。

文成默表示，金正恩视察核设施也可能意在检查国家核计划目标今年取得了哪些进展，以及在年底劳动党会议之前必须设定哪些未来目标。

韩国国防部表示，韩方严肃对待金正恩关于战场核武器的言论，并补充说，首尔在韩美同盟下对平壤的核威胁保持坚定的军事戒备。韩国联合参谋本部拒绝分享对朝中社报道的朝鲜核设施的分析，称这是韩国和美国的机密信息。

特朗普仍希望与金正恩会面。特朗普上周访问中国出席亚太经济合作组织峰会时重申了他恢复与金正恩外交的渴望。但特朗普与金正恩的会面并未发生，平壤没有公开回应特朗普的提议。

本周在接受《纽约邮报》采访时，特朗普驳斥了金正恩拒绝其示好的说法，称：“不，他没有无视。你知道，我们在那里有很多领导人……总会有我们见面的时候……只是当时时机不太合适。那是非常忙碌的两天。”

特朗普还声称，他随时可以通过重启他们在其第一个任期内保持的信件往来来恢复与金正恩的外交，尽管他承认两位领导人“最近”没有通信。

金正恩此前曾表示，如果美国放弃对朝鲜的“敌对政策”并尊重他所称的朝鲜核国家地位，他就可以重返谈判。专家表示，金正恩旨在赢得国际社会对其核国家地位的承认，以便要求解除国际制裁。

上周，国际原子能机构总干事拉斐尔·格罗西评估称，朝鲜一直在扩建其位于宁边的原有铀浓缩设施，称此举“令人严重关切”。

核武器可以用高浓缩铀或武器级钚制造，朝鲜在宁边拥有生产这两种材料的设施。去年，韩国统一部长官郑东泳表示，朝鲜运营着四个铀浓缩设施，且每天都在运行。

Good morning. You're reading the Up First newsletter. Subscribe here to get it delivered to your inbox, and listen to the Up First podcast for all the news you need to start your day.

Today's top stories

Severe storms sweeping across the nation threaten to cause widespread travel delays today, as millions of people gather with their loved ones. New York City officials announced that the Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade has been rescheduled to Saturday due to the threat of powerful wind gusts that could reach up to 60 mph. This year marked the 100th procession, and the first time the iconic event is being postponed.

Workers inflate the Spider-Man balloon during Macy's Balloon Inflation 2026 on November 25, 2026 in New York City. Macy's plans to celebrate its 100th Thanksgiving Day Parade with a record 100 inflatables, but forecasted high winds are threatening to ground the giant balloons.

Adam Gray/Getty Images

hide caption

Adam Gray/Getty Images

• 🎧 Something is happening across almost every part of the country right now, NPR's Kat Lonsdorf tells Up First. Extreme high tides are affecting the West Coast, snow is expected in parts of the Midwest, and in the South and Southeast, a major storm is advancing up the East Coast. Meteorologist Richard Bann with the National Weather Service Weather Prediction Center tells Lonsdorf the East Coast storm is the primary concern. Bann says the storm will become better organized throughout the day, bringing strong winds and heavy rain that could lead to coastal flooding. The good news: Forecasters expect the East Coast's major storm to move on, mostly wrapping up by Saturday, Lonsdorf says.

The Trump administration has proposed new tariffs targeting goods from 14 major U.S. trading partners, including China, Japan and the European Union. Administration officials argue the measures counter unfair foreign trade practices, though critics question their ultimate effectiveness. Proposed rates may reach 40% on Chinese imports, 35% on Vietnamese goods, and 20-25% on products from other targeted nations. Additional tariffs on Brazilian sugar and aircraft are also being suggested.

• 🎧 U.S. Trade Ambassador Jamieson Greer said that new tariffs could take effect within a couple of months. For each country, the White House has listed a "proposed" rate and a "deal" rate, NPR's Danielle Kurtzleben says. For example, if talks with China progress positively, they may receive a deal rate of 20%, which is different from its proposed rate of 40%. Although the Supreme Court overturned President Trump's previous tariffs, the new ones fall under Section 301, a law meant to counter unfair trade practices. The administration says these countries exhibit "structural excess capacity" in various manufactured goods, a situation caused by policies that lead to overproduction, which can distort the global market.

Federal scientists are testing the air, soil and water in Eastern Iowa for lead contamination after the U.S. Army detonated thousands of pounds of unstable lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown yesterday. Officials said the controlled explosion was the only safe way to dispose of the bomb-making compound.

• 🎧 Eliza Billingham of NPR network station Iowa Public Radio says the major concern is the potential release of lead into the air from the explosion. She adds that the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency has tested the area since the detonation and hasn't found lead in the air. The EPA has deployed around 300 people to sample the air, ground and nearby water. Lead is a neurotoxin that especially endangers children and pregnant people because it can impede childhood development. After a week and a half of delays and inconsistent communication from the Army, residents have grown hesitant about the Army and the EPA's initial findings, Billingham says. Residents want independent monitoring and the University of Iowa and the University of Illinois are conducting regional sampling. Results are expected in a few days and should show if their measurements align with the EPA's data, Billingham says.

A federal judge has blocked Trump from challenging the ABC television network's broadcast licenses. U.S. District Court Judge Loren AliKhan ruled that the president retaliating against satire and commentary he dislikes is unconstitutional. AliKhan issued the preliminary injunction yesterday and dismissed the administration's request to throw out ABC and Disney's lawsuit challenging the review of the local license. Licenses typically last eight years and are rarely revoked. AliKhan's decision drew heavily on Trump's public statements and social media posts against ABC and Disney, as well as comments from Brendan Carr, the president's pick for chair of the Federal Communications Commission.

Life advice

Our brains are wired to seek out newness, and the retail industry is set up to keep us coming back for more as quickly as possible.

J Studios/Getty Images

hide caption

J Studios/Getty Images

Holiday shopping season is in full swing. Before you spend, consider if you actually need what's in your cart. Sales are exciting because our brains are wired to seek newness. Retailers capitalize on that urge. To escape the cycle of constantly wanting more, shop intentionally and appreciate what you already own, says Eric Athas, author of Saying No to New. He shares his insights on breaking this cycle and finding joy in your current possessions with Life Kit.

• 🛒 Delete the app or remove your credit card info if you have one-click checkout with a company.

• 🛒 Add an item to your online shopping cart and leave it for 24 hours. Research shows that delaying a purchase decreases your interest in it.

• 🛒 Make intentional choices. Don't reject all new things. After you understand this, you can learn to say no to the wrong items and yes to the right ones.

• 🛒 Revisiting old things can provide you with untapped enjoyment in them, research has found. You can apply this by rereading a book or by traveling to a city you have visited before.

For more guidance on how to reclaim joy without seeking newness, listen to this episode of NPR's Life Kit. Subscribe to the Life Kit newsletter for expert advice on love, money, relationships and more.

Apple farmers across the Pacific Northwest are ripping out thousands of acres of orchards and grinding trees into mulch because growing the fruit no longer pays. Many say they're being crushed by soaring labor and equipment costs and international tariffs. Even multigenerational growers are leaving land unused rather than hemorrhaging money. Thousands of acres of fruit have been left to rot unpicked on branches, pushing some well-established farms into bankruptcy. Federal farm relief has also largely failed to reach specialty-crop growers. Take a look at photos and videos of affected farms, and read more about how the region that supplies the majority of the U.S.' fresh apples is handling the challenge.

2. The Ariston Cafe opened in 1924 along Illinois's Route 66, serving classic American diner fare. The National Register landmark attracts international travelers and hosts local milestones, from wedding proposals to 65th anniversaries.

Watch: BBC confronts German man suspected of supplying migrant gangs with small boats

Watch: BBC confronts German man suspected of supplying migrant gangs with small boats

A German boat dealer is suspected of being a key supplier to migrant smugglers operating in the English Channel, the BBC can reveal.

Nearly a third of small-boat crossings to the UK, in the first four months of 2026, allegedly involved boats or engines from MaReBoote, a small firm in western Germany, according to files we have seen.

The managing director, Marvin Reuter, is contesting extradition to France, where he could face smuggling, criminal conspiracy and involuntary manslaughter charges.

His equipment is suspected of being linked to two fatal accidents, in which four men died.

We confronted the 35-year-old at his business, but he would not answer our questions. He said he was reporting us to the police.

items.title: How American Thanksgiving took root — and evolved — in Liberia
items.summary: The first settlers of Liberia were African Americans who brought along the holiday of Thanksgiving — which has evolved to reflect the history and identity of this new nation.
items.body:
Global Health

How American Thanksgiving took root — and evolved — in Liberia

November 25, 20269:14 AM ET

Ari Daniel

Yvonne Capehart Weah's family routinely gets together in the township where she grew up in Liberia. In early November every year, they gather to celebrate the Liberian version of Thanksgiving.

Eddie Raynes

hide caption

Eddie Raynes

Yvonne Capehart Weah is from Liberia, a country in West Africa, and she's one of twelve siblings.

"I'm the second to the last one — I'm the eleventh," she says. "We have large families in Liberia."

Every year on the first Thursday in November, Weah's family gathers in Caldwell, the township where she grew up, to celebrate Liberian Thanksgiving.

"When we come together, the group become [so] large that you are not able to sit around a dining table," she explains. "So we do it outside under the tree. And when we meet, it's almost like we're having a party."

The Liberian holiday dates back to the first half of the 19th century when the American Colonization Society established the community that would grow into the country. It was founded by Black Americans — both those born free and enslaved people who had been emancipated — whose departure was sometimes voluntary, sometimes forced. "The settlers from America brought that Thanksgiving Day tradition to Liberia," says Weah. Once transplanted, the holiday evolved over time in response to national events.

Liberia gained its independence in 1847 but the British continued trying to take swaths of territory. In 1883, President Alfred Francis Russell, an Episcopalian priest, called upon God to help halt the incursions.

That invocation was a "prayer of protection against the intruders, preventing intrusion into our territory," says Weah.

The Liberians managed to maintain their sovereignty. And that year, the legislature officially established Thanksgiving as a national holiday steeped in the religious gratitude of the moment.

A sacred day for all

Weah summarizes Liberian Thanksgiving this way: "It's giving thanks to God for our freedom, for divine protection. It's giving thanks to God for unity and for the harvest."

Weah says that her family's celebration, like that of many others in Liberia, starts in the morning at church. But the holiday's for people of all faiths, and other religious communities mark the occasion as well

"The Muslims, they go to the mosques and pray," says Sekou Muhammad Sheriff, a YouTuber who travels his home country of Liberia to showcase its offerings and cultural heritage, including Thanksgiving. "And Muslims, Christians, and others — everybody observe this day as a holiday."

When Sheriff was a boy, this was the day that he counted on to get a new outfit.

"What my dad used to do for me," says Sheriff, was to purchase a "shirt-trouser suit, and then he'd buy me slipper." His favorite suit was a white one.

Over the years on Thanksgiving, he's grown accustomed to eating different stews, including one made with sweet potato leaves and another with snails collected from the garden.

"We call it king's meat," Sheriff says with a chuckle. "It is very, very nice."

The mid-afternoon meal varies from household to household in Liberia.

Yvonne Capehart Weah's nieces and nephews fill their plates at a family gathering in Caldwell.

Rebecca Blapoh Weah

hide caption

Rebecca Blapoh Weah

"We don't do turkey," says Weah, "but we do chicken. We do fried chicken, smoked chicken, roasted chicken."

Weah's family also serves jollof rice, watermelon, pineapple and a variety of stews, including one called fufu and soup. It's a mix of cassava, fish, chicken, okra, chili pepper and more. "That makes the soup very tasty," says Weah. "It has to be [at] every Thanksgiving."

(Weah doesn't especially like to cook, however. "If you tell me, 'Go in the kitchen to cook or sit in the living room and read,'" she says, "I will sit in the living room and read.")

"I'm thanking God"

This year, Sheriff didn't have the resources to host Thanksgiving. But he says that he remains thankful to God for keeping him healthy and for keeping Liberia peaceful after civil conflict tore his country apart from 1989 to 1997 and 1999 to 2003.

Weah is also grateful. "When I go for Thanksgiving," she says, "I'm thanking God for where I have come from, where I am now, and I'm also thanking Him for where He will take me because I know He holds the future."

Weah is the program manager at the We-Care Foundation, an education nonprofit that, among other things, teaches children literacy. "A reading child will become a reading elder," she says.

"And we expect informed adults to make informed decisions that affect both their social and economic life" — in ways, perhaps, that they will one day be thankful for.

Yvonne Capehart Weah's family routinely gets together in the township where she grew up in Liberia. In early November every year, they gather to celebrate the Liberian version of Thanksgiving.

Eddie Raynes

hide caption
Eddie Raynes
Yvonne Capehart Weah is from Liberia, a country in West Africa, and she's one of twelve siblings.
"I'm the second to the last one — I'm the eleventh," she says. "We have large families in Liberia."
Every year on the first Thursday in November, Weah's family gathers in Caldwell, the township where she grew up, to celebrate Liberian Thanksgiving.

"When we come together, the group become [so] large that you are not able to sit around a dining table," she explains. "So we do it outside under the tree. And when we meet, it's almost like we're having a party."

The Liberian holiday dates back to the first half of the 19th century when the American Colonization Society established the community that would grow into the country. It was founded by Black Americans — both those born free and enslaved people who had been emancipated — whose departure was sometimes voluntary, sometimes forced. "The settlers from America brought that Thanksgiving Day tradition to Liberia," says Weah. Once transplanted, the holiday evolved over time in response to national events.

Liberia gained its independence in 1847 but the British continued trying to take swaths of territory. In 1883, President Alfred Francis Russell, an Episcopalian priest, called upon God to help halt the incursions.
That invocation was a "prayer of protection against the intruders, preventing intrusion into our territory," says Weah.
The Liberians managed to maintain their sovereignty. And that year, the legislature officially established Thanksgiving as a national holiday steeped in the religious gratitude of the moment.
A sacred day for all
Weah summarizes Liberian Thanksgiving this way: "It's giving thanks to God for our freedom, for divine protection. It's giving thanks to God for unity and for the harvest."

Weah says that her family's celebration, like that of many others in Liberia, starts in the morning at church. But the holiday's for people of all faiths, and other religious communities mark the occasion as well

"The Muslims, they go to the mosques and pray," says Sekou Muhammad Sheriff, a YouTuber who travels his home country of Liberia to showcase its offerings and cultural heritage, including Thanksgiving. "And Muslims, Christians, and others — everybody observe this day as a holiday."
When Sheriff was a boy, this was the day that he counted on to get a new outfit.
"What my dad used to do for me," says Sheriff, was to purchase a "shirt-trouser suit, and then he'd buy me slipper." His favorite suit was a white one.
Over the years on Thanksgiving, he's grown accustomed to eating different stews, including one made with sweet potato leaves and another with snails collected from the garden.
"We call it king's meat," Sheriff says with a chuckle. "It is very, very nice."
The mid-afternoon meal varies from household to household in Liberia.

blocks.text:
Yvonne Capehart Weah's nieces and nephews fill their plates at a family gathering in Caldwell.

Rebecca Blapoh Weah

hide caption
Rebecca Blapoh Weah
"We don't do turkey," says Weah, "but we do chicken. We do fried chicken, smoked chicken, roasted chicken."

Weah's family also serves jollof rice, watermelon, pineapple and a variety of stews, including one called fufu and soup. It's a mix of cassava, fish, chicken, okra, chili pepper and more. "That makes the soup very tasty," says Weah. "It has to be [at] every Thanksgiving."
(Weah doesn't especially like to cook, however. "If you tell me, 'Go in the kitchen to cook or sit in the living room and read,'" she says, "I will sit in the living room and read.")
"I'm thanking God"

This year, Sheriff didn't have the resources to host Thanksgiving. But he says that he remains thankful to God for keeping him healthy and for keeping Liberia peaceful after civil conflict tore his country apart from 1989 to 1997 and 1999 to 2003.

Weah is also grateful. "When I go for Thanksgiving," she says, "I'm thanking God for where I have come from, where I am now, and I'm also thanking Him for where He will take me because I know He holds the future."
Weah is the program manager at the We-Care Foundation, an education nonprofit that, among other things, teaches children literacy. "A reading child will become a reading elder," she says.
"And we expect informed adults to make informed decisions that affect both their social and economic life" — in ways, perhaps, that they will one day be thankful for.

美国感恩节如何在利比里亚扎根并演变

2026年11月25日上午9:14（美国东部时间）

阿里·丹尼尔

伊冯娜·卡普哈特·维亚的家人经常在她成长的利比里亚小镇聚会。每年11月初，他们聚在一起庆祝利比里亚版的感恩节。

埃迪·雷恩斯

隐藏图注

埃迪·雷恩斯

伊冯娜·卡普哈特·维亚来自西非国家利比里亚，她是十二个兄弟姐妹之一。

“我是倒数第二个——我排第十一，”她说。“利比里亚的家庭都很大。”

每年11月的第一个星期四，维亚的家人都会聚集在她成长的考德威尔镇，庆祝利比里亚感恩节。

“我们聚在一起时，队伍变得[太]庞大，你没法围坐在餐桌旁，”她解释道。“所以我们就在外面的树下聚会。我们相聚时，几乎就像在开派对。”

这个利比里亚节日可追溯到19世纪上半叶，当时美国殖民协会建立了后来发展成这个国家的社区。它由美国黑人创立——既有生来自由的黑人，也有被解放的奴隶——他们的离开有时是自愿的，有时是被迫的。“来自美国的定居者把那个感恩节传统带到了利比里亚，”维亚说。这一节日移植过来后，随着时间推移，因应国家事件而不断演变。

利比里亚于1847年获得独立，但英国继续试图夺取大片领土。1883年，身为圣公会牧师的总统阿尔弗雷德·弗朗西斯·拉塞尔祈求上帝帮助阻止入侵。

那次祈祷是“祈求保护、抵御入侵者，防止他们侵入我们的领土，”维亚说。

利比里亚人成功维护了主权。那一年，立法机构正式将感恩节确立为全国性节日，浸透着当时宗教性的感恩之情。

对所有人都是神圣的日子

维亚这样概括利比里亚感恩节：“这是感谢上帝赐予我们自由、赐予神圣庇护。这是感谢上帝赐予团结和丰收。”

维亚说，她家的庆祝活动与利比里亚许多家庭一样，从早上去教堂开始。但这个节日属于所有信仰的人，其他宗教群体也会纪念这个日子。

“穆斯林去清真寺祈祷，”塞库·穆罕默德·谢里夫说。他是一位YouTuber，走遍家乡利比里亚，展示当地的风物和文化遗产，包括感恩节。“穆斯林、基督徒和其他人——所有人都把这一天当作节日来庆祝。”

谢里夫小时候，这一天是他指望能添置新衣的日子。

“我爸爸过去会给我做的是，”谢里夫说，买一套“衬衫长裤套装，然后他会给我买拖鞋。”他最喜欢的套装是白色的。

多年来在感恩节，他渐渐习惯了吃各种炖菜，包括一种用红薯叶做的，还有一种用从园子里收集的蜗牛做的。

“我们叫它国王的肉，”谢里夫笑着说。“非常非常好吃。”

在利比里亚，下午三四点的那顿正餐各家不同。

伊冯娜·卡普哈特·维亚的侄女和侄子们在考德威尔的一次家庭聚会上盛满自己的盘子。

丽贝卡·布拉波·维亚

隐藏图注

丽贝卡·布拉波·维亚

“我们不吃火鸡，”维亚说，“但我们吃鸡。我们做炸鸡、熏鸡、烤鸡。”

维亚家还供应乔洛夫米饭、西瓜、菠萝和各种炖菜，包括一种叫富富配汤的。它是木薯、鱼、鸡、秋葵、辣椒等的混合。“这让汤非常美味，”维亚说。“每顿感恩节都[必须]有。”

（不过维亚并不特别喜欢做饭。“如果你对我说，‘去厨房做饭，还是坐在客厅看书，’”她说，“我会坐在客厅看书。”）

“我感谢上帝”

今年，谢里夫没有资源操办感恩节。但他说，他仍然感谢上帝让他保持健康，让利比里亚在1989年至1997年以及1999年至2003年的内战撕裂国家之后保持和平。

维亚也心怀感激。“我去过感恩节时，”她说，“我感谢上帝我从哪里来、我现在在哪里，我也感谢祂将带我去哪里，因为我知道祂掌管未来。”

维亚是We-Care基金会的项目经理，这是一家教育非营利组织，除其他工作外，还教儿童识字。“爱读书的孩子会成为爱读书的长者，”她说。

“我们期望知情的成年人做出知情的决定，影响他们的社会和经济生活”——或许，以他们有一天会心怀感激的方式。
